items.title: Tell HN: I unknowingly broke the PHP RCE embargo. I am sorry.
items.author: petecooper
items.text:
I posted here about the then-upcoming PHP RCEs related to CVE-2026-109618 & CVE-2026-109619. I appreciate this has had considerable knock-on effects with the schedule for co-ordinated disclosure, and created additional workload.

I am truly sorry. I take full responsibility for my actions.

It was not remotely my intention to cause any of the subsequent side effects.

At the time of posting, I didn't know about any embargo. My contact had told me there was no embargo, and her contact had told her the same thing.

As someone who follows the 4-weekly PHP release cycle and compiles it from source, my intention was to alert others in a similar position to be aware of the importance/urgency of the updates.

That clearly backfired in a pretty wild fashion. I have learned my lesson.

items.title: Show HN: Uberblok – an interactive museum of ZFS internals
items.author: storagebits
items.text:
I've worked for a long time in the storage field during my career and ZFS is the piece of engineering I admire most in that space. I wanted a way to pay homage to it and to explore and better understand its internals. So I built Uberblok: a museum of ZFS. A deep dive into copy-on-write, txgs, vdevs, RAID-Z, snapshots, the ARC, metaslabs, the ZIL, send/receive with explanations and animated diagrams.

I'm sure people here know these internals better than I do, so corrections are very welcome.

I built it with my agent swarm organization, Algotitan.

I hope you'll enjoy the deep dive into Uberblok as much as I do.

Museum: https://uberblok.storagebits.workers.dev Repo: https://github.com/algotitanhq/uberblok

items.title: Show HN: Replacing CAPTCHAs with adaptive proof-of-work in WordPress
items.author: MatthiasNordwig
items.text:
When I founded my business a whistle-blowing-service for enterprises, I’ve seeked for a working solution to block spam bots on that home page. The solution was intended to comply with EU data privacy law, no cookies, no sniffing, light-weight-size, on my webserver only, beeing invisible for my site visitors and no running costs at all.

I came across Hashcash, a proof-of-work approach, to block spam. When I implemented it, it worked immediately and blocked 100 percent without blocking any incoming real posts.

I was astonished, that no solution existed in the ecosystem allready that covered all forms and was for free. Therefore I‘ve turned it into a free wordpress-plugin.

It is not only a technical solution, but starts with the business model of spam (mass spamming at low cost), by producing a calculation effort for every single post, that unavoidable. And therefore is not exactly unbreakable but becomes very expensive for the spammer and therefore alows only for targeted high quality approaches that need other treatment. Up to now my own page remains spam free and users report the same.

Now, running since 2022 on 4000+ active installations, it is working with almost every webform and plugin combination that is running on any wordpress instance, using pattern recognition on http-post-level instead of specific proprietary integration for single specific form builders. It ships with 80+ starting patterns for the most relevant form builders and themes, but can be enhanced with any pattern by the user.

The plugin can be previewed directly and immediately on wordpress.org. It ships with14 KB compressed under a GPL-2.0 license.

I’m looking forward to discuss about the proof-of-work approach, form detection, privacy implications, and tradeoffs.

items.title: Show HN: CATT 0.2.1: Test agents/services against a Muse/Instinct-alike, in CI
items.author: botacode
items.text:
Hey HN, we recently open sourced our Consumer Agent Testing Tool to help teams iterate against proprietary assistants like Muse and Instinct. We built this to reduce our own frustrations with building an MCP/API for these agents to consume.

The problem: testing against these tools is hard! Agent memory + account statefulness make reproducibility, in the ways required for repeatable/reliable outcomes, between agents and the APIs/MCPs they interact with very challenging.

The solution: CATT lets devs test their services against a surrogate Muse or Instinct agent (not affiliated with either of these companies). Testers define starting conditions, approvals, and success conditions for their service's state. CATT then records the full interaction (incl. tool calls, responses) so it can diff what happened from what the agent reports. Runs can be tested in local builds or via CI, with or without LLM backing.

CATT is designed to emulate the important parts of personal assistant interactions. Its got:

- Tool calls and command-line tool access - Simulated approvals for service actions - Outcomes tracking and comparison - Optional MCP profile based on an unofficial Muse template

There are limitations to how much we know about different assistant specific behaviors so the tool labels its assumptions as `documented`, `unofficial`, `assumed` or `unknown` for developer review. We'll do our best to keep the tool updated as new insights about the internal workings of these assistants come to light. It is an area of active research and interest, a good example is this recent report on how Instinct uses Exa for web search [0].

Are you building a connector or MCP? If yes, we'd like to hear from you! Have you had assistants behave incoherently, use stale information, or procalim success without evidence? What else should we add tests for?

The best way to get started is...to point your coding assistant at the repo and ask it to integrate the tool with your CI or local testing pipeline!

Hope it's helpful!

[0]: https://www.sunbeam.ai/thoughts/instinct-is-using-exa-for-we...

items.title: Show HN: Dovepass – can I legally fly a drone along this exact path in SF?
items.author: nimitmehra
items.text:
Dovepass answers one question for drone operators: given two points, can a drone legally fly between the two points?

I build route planning for delivery drivers and wanted to check what it would look like if the vehicle flies. Drone navigation is different from land-based vehicle navigation. In addition to road and traffic data, it requires data on buildings, building height, wind speed and direction, and total load, including the payload a drone might carry. It is also governed by a set of rules; depending on the area, federal, state, or county rules may apply.

The decision point becomes whether, at each point on the route the drone can fly based upon whether regulations permit, the wind direction favours it and whether it flying over a road or people? Depending on when the drone flies, the same path valid two hours ago may no longer be valid.

For example a trip from 24th & Valencia ( Mission) to 19th Ave & Irving (Inner Sunset) and back is 5.1 km each way. A DJI mini 4 Pro would take 19 min on 7 mph winds from the west and use 92% of its usable battery and give a Go signal with warning. But at 11mph wind from the same direction would become No-Go because it would use 111% of its usable battery. Or whenever there is a Giants game at Oracle Park, this route is unusable because it is 2.5miles from the stadium. FAA bars all drones within 3 nautical miles from a stadium from 1 hour before the game to one hour after it ends.

I chose San Francisco as the first city to build this because there is enough data about the buildings (92% coverage), wind data is easily available at the drone flying height, and the city has a mix of slopes, water bodies, buildings and airport-related airspace restrictions all in one city. The city also has local rules regarding drone flights in parks - both operated by the city as well as by Golden Gate National recreational areas ( National Park Service).

I used kimi to build it and claude acted a sa judge. To understand more about the challenges faced during the build and the tradeoffs made please read - https://dovepass.com/how-it-was-built/"

items.title: Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
items.author: kmansm27
items.text:
Hey all, Kartik from Omnara (https://omnara.com) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API.

You may remember us from our early days, when we made a remote-control phone app for Claude Code and Codex. Since the harness ran on a laptop back then, we had to build a relay to reach it, it stopped when the laptop closed, and moving it to a cloud sandbox meant syncing code and agent state between machines. We didn't think remote-controlling a local agent was end-game for how people would run agents, so we built a new product where the agent runs in the cloud, any client can talk to it through an API, and it can still use your laptop as one of its machines.

Anthropic and OpenAI are building hosted versions of this, like Claude Managed Agents and the OpenAI Agents API. Omnara is an open-source version you can run on your own servers and use your own models. It's basically a harness server like the opencode or codex servers, but durable, scalable, with the usual harness features like file and shell tools, subagents, compaction, permission prompts, MCP, skills, memory, yada yada yada.

Here's some interesting architectural decisions we made while building this out:

Most harnesses, like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Goose, etc, run the agent loop in one long-lived process that keeps its log in a JSONL or SQLite file. In Omnara, the log is an append-only event log in Postgres, with inputs, model outputs and tool calls stored as typed rows in their own tables. The loop runs on stateless workers in the control plane. A worker runs one iteration of the loop, either a model call or the tool calls it produced, then releases the agent and puts the next iteration on a queue in Postgres. Whichever worker is free picks it up, so each iteration of an agent's loop can run in a different process on a different machine. Each iteration's result commits in one transaction, so the model output, its tool calls, usage and the next wakeup are saved together or not at all. If a worker dies mid-iteration, nothing commits, its lease expires, and another worker retries it. Agents waiting on a user, a tool or a retry don't hold a worker, so one worker can multiplex thousands of agents.

Also unlike other harnesses, the machines that the workers (our agent loop) run on aren't where the agent runs its commands. Instead, any macOS or Linux machine with an internet connection, like your laptop or any cloud sandbox, can run a small daemon (omnarad) that connects out to Omnara, so it doesn't need any open inbound ports. The agent then gets tools for that machine, like running a command or editing a file. An agent can have any number of machines connected to it. A fun thing I like to do is I have my laptop and a cloud sandbox connected to the same agent, so when my laptop is on, my agent codes there and I can interact with it, and I have it often push to Github. When I close my laptop, my agent sees the laptop went offline, pulls the latest changes to its cloud sandbox, and continues there.

The entire codebase is open source at https://github.com/omnara-ai/omnara, and it’s self hostable, even on a single machine with docker compose. You can also use the hosted version at https://omnara.com. Let me know what you think!

items.title: Launch HN: Alter (YC S25) – Access control for multi-user agents
items.author: simfinii
items.text:
Hi HN! We’re Srikar and Kevan, founders of Alter – https://alterauth.com/. We’re building access control for agents that can take actions on behalf of multiple users.

If you’ve built an internal agent people use through Slack, you may have experienced this scenario: everyone signs in with their own account, but the agent connects to the CRM or billing system with one shared API key, so the agent can do anything that the key can do. User-level authentication in Slack does nothing to control what the agent can do in an external system like the CRM or billing system.

Here’s what Alter does:

-It acts as a proxy and manages downstream credentials for every API request that an agent takes;

-It takes identity into account for every action the agent does. Automatically take into account the end user identity of the person that the agent is taking actions on behalf of.

-It enforces fine grained runtime policies and records compliance grade audit logs.

Here’s a demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ZqPU14ipGE

We started this because we saw first hand how hard it is to build agents in regulated industries. To unlock the true benefits of agents we need to allow agents to take actions, sometimes actions on behalf of end users. I (Srikar) was working at Goldmans and I saw how prohibitively expensive it was for me as a developer to write my own custom auth to enable multi-tenancy in agents and to allow agents to have strict policy controls as they act on behalf of end users. My co-founder, Kevan, is a second time founder and was previously working on a database startup. He has experience building and selling deep tech into highly regulated environments. So this problem seemed like a natural fit for the both of us.

Building and maintaining custom auth for multi tenant agents was challenging. But so was ensuring that the solution we developed was secure, scalable and keeping track of security grade audit logs. As a result we realized there needs to be a separate product category for this that enables developers to easily build secure multi user agents that can actually take actions in an enterprise. Some of the real-world use cases we’ve seen include:

We have built a multi user open claw for our own team using Alter that saved us countless hours on our GTM effort. Link here:https://github.com/AlterAIDev/openclaw-alter-plugin

We have multiple startups who have used our platform to build their own secure internal agents for everything ranging from SRE agents to back office agents dealing with Quickbooks and payroll platforms like Rippling. It has saved developers countless hours both in terms of building and maintenance. We also have a defense contractor building air gapped agents for marine corp using Alter.

Under the hood, the value that we provide is that we do a lot of the plumbing that no one wants to do. We support hundreds of providers, all manually tested end to end. Reliability is our biggest priority. We have built this in a way to allow developers to custom build their agents however they see fit. Everything ranging from custom policies, agent delegation, user attribution, audit logs needed for compliance to a LLM gateway with guardrails (Coming soon)

Building a security product is hard. We have learnt that in order to build a truly secure product, security thinking has to pervade every part of the development process. We have embraced shift left security. Every PR that is pushed out is continuously checked for supply chain attacks, potentially dangerous code patterns etc.

Our business plan revolved around usage based pricing. There is a free tier up to 10k requests and then a pricing tier starting beyond that. We would love it if people configured their APIs and OAuth credentials, tried out the policies and actually built agents that can take actions with alter!

If you’ve built an agent that acts for multiple users, how are you handling permissions today? We’d especially like to hear what you’ve had to build yourself.

https://alterauth.com/

items.title: Show HN: OnKey – I'm a bad singer, so I built an app to show where I'm off-key
items.author: dsmurrell
items.text:
Hi all

I was pretty terrible at singing, now I’d say I’m bad but not terrible. This is because I’ve been using a singing app (won’t name it here) that scores me on my pitch and timing throughout the song so that I can improve.

Lately however, the app I’ve been using has flooded their song list with songs that aren’t originals. I didn’t like this at all as for me, it’s easier to try to improve when you’re singing along to the original.

So, I asked an agent (Claude Code) if it could write some code to listen to Spotify and also listen to me and see if it could detect both pitches and score me. It impressed me by writing some Python and showing me my pitch in the terminal!

It couldn’t go all the way though and detect the singer’s pitch in real time.

So I found the next best setup and built OnKey, a Mac app that needs to listen to the song once (it doesn’t save it) and then when it’s learnt the song (takes a couple of minutes), you can sing along to the pitch track that it’s learnt. OnKey is free to use and open source under the MIT license.

It can listen to Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube playing in your browser with the right permissions.

During the build I found that someone had done something similar in Nightingale, but this requires a library of songs exported to disk and who has this in 2026 (maybe some of you ;) - but we need to help the normies too).

You can check out a demo video on the site of me singing (warning given) here: https://singonkey.app

The app sends out to find the song info (short Shazam fingerprint, and looks up song details), lyrics (from LRCLIB), and checks for updates.

The app never sends the music (it doesn’t save this to disk) and your voice. Everything you’d expect to stay private does.

It’s still weak in a few places:

- when the song’s backing is noisy it’s hard to pick the pitch track out

- sometimes it gets a note an octave off

- it’s limited to Apple Silicon Macs, M1 or later, and only macOS 14.2 up because extra drivers aren’t required past this point

- the scoring is built for beginners like me so it’s fairly easy on you

Would love for people to try it out and let me know what works and what doesn’t for them!
